prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
We aim to resolve the limitations of current single-view 3D hair reconstruction methods, which struggle to produce high-fidelity, diverse hairstyles. Existing approaches typically rely on sparse "guide strands" and low-dimensional scalp embeddings to cope with the scarcity of paired 3D training data. This compression creates a bottleneck: models fail to capture intricate spatial relationships between strands, leading to over-smoothed results that cannot represent complex geometries like tightly curled or afro-textured hair. Furthermore, these methods require heuristic post-processing (upsampling and noise injection) to densify the hair, which often results in unrealistic artifacts.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can bypass the limitations of guide strands and heuristic upsampling by formulating hair generation as a 2D texture synthesis problem. We propose that a dense "scalp texture"—where every pixel explicitly contains the latent geometric code for a single hair strand—can be learned and generated by a diffusion model. By training on a massive procedural dataset, we believe a diffusion transformer conditioned on robust image features can directly predict the geometry of hundreds of thousands of individual strands, effectively capturing high-frequency details and varying hair densities without needing post-processing.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

**1. Data-Driven Strategy**
To overcome the lack of real-world paired data, we will first develop a procedural generation pipeline to create a massive synthetic dataset. This will combine parametric geometric operations (clumping, curling, noise) to produce diverse 3D hairstyles paired with photorealistic renderings.

**2. Canonical Scalp Representation**
We will convert 3D hair data into a 2D representation suitable for image-based generative models:
*   **Strand Encoding:** We will train an autoencoder to compress the geometry of individual hair strands into compact latent codes.
*   **Neural Scalp Texture:** These latent codes will be painted onto a UV map of the scalp. Consequently, any specific location on this texture map will store the geometric DNA of the strand growing at that point.
*   **Density Mapping:** We will simultaneously model a probability map defining the likelihood of hair existence at each texel, allowing us to naturally handle variable densities (e.g., baldness or sparse regions).

**3. Conditional Diffusion Framework**
We will design an image-conditioned diffusion model to synthesize these scalp textures:
*   **Architecture:** We will utilize a diffusion transformer optimized for pixel-space generation to denoise the scalp texture and density map.
*   **Semantic Conditioning:** Instead of relying on low-level orientation filters (which fail under occlusion), we will extract deep semantic features from the input image using a pre-trained vision backbone. These features will guide the diffusion process via cross-attention, ensuring the generated texture aligns with the visual evidence.
*   **Perceptual Loss Weighting:** To ensure the model prioritizes geometric features that matter visually (like curl curvature), we will implement a loss weighting strategy based on the perceptual impact of the latent code dimensions.

**4. Direct Decoding**
For inference, the diffusion model will predict a clean scalp texture and density map. We will generate the final 3D asset by probabilistically sampling points on the scalp according to the density map, extracting the latent codes from those coordinates, and decoding them directly into full-resolution 3D strands.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Theoretical Shift:** Moving the field away from sparse guide-strand interpolation toward dense, direct strand synthesis.
*   **Geometric Fidelity:** Enabling the reconstruction of challenging hair types (specifically afro-textured and curly hair) that are currently impossible for state-of-the-art methods.
*   **Unified Density Modeling:** Providing a mechanism to naturally handle topology changes, such as male pattern baldness, which are often ignored by fixed-topology models.
*   **End-to-End Simplicity:** Demonstrating that 3D hair can be generated directly for real-time engines without requiring complex post-processing or simulation heuristics.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We designed and executed a series of experiments to evaluate a novel diffusion-based framework ("DiffLocks") for generating 3D hair from single images. The system utilized a "scalp texture" representation where each pixel contained a latent code for an individual hair strand.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **Training Dataset (Synthetic):** We generated a custom dataset containing 40,000 unique samples.
        *   *Content:* Each sample included a 3D hairstyle ($\approx 100,000$ strands) and a corresponding RGB image ($768 \times 768$ resolution) rendered via path tracing.
        *   *Generation Pipeline:* We utilized Blender geometry nodes starting from 75 manually created base hairstyles. Variations included interpolation, clumping, curling, noise, and physics simulation (cloth/wind/gravity).
        *   *Scene Diversity:* We used 255 HDRIs for lighting, randomized exposure/angle, and applied random textures/expressions to SMPL-X bodies. Camera focal lengths were randomized between 40mm and 150mm.
    *   **Evaluation Dataset 1 (External):** Selected straight and curly medium-length hairstyles from the synthetic dataset of Yuksel et al.
        *   *Rendering:* To avoid bias towards our path-traced training data, we rendered these evaluation images using Unreal Engine.
    *   **Evaluation Dataset 2 (Internal):** We created a "DiffLocks evaluation set" containing 10 representative hairstyles generated via our Blender pipeline, specifically to test variety not present in existing public datasets.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **3D Reconstruction Accuracy:** We measured Precision, Recall, and F-score.
    *   **Thresholds:** We reported these metrics at three strictness levels of spatial and angular alignment:
        1.  2mm / 20 degrees
        2.  3mm / 30 degrees
        3.  4mm / 40 degrees
    *   **Runtime Performance:** Total inference time measured in seconds, broken down by pipeline stage.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **NeuralHDHair:** A state-of-the-art single-view reconstruction method.
    *   **HairStep:** A state-of-the-art single-view reconstruction method.
    *   **HAAR:** A generative text-to-hair method. For comparison, we adapted this for image-to-hair by using LLaVA to generate text descriptions from the input images, which were then fed into HAAR.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Hardware:** All runtime evaluations were performed on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU.
    *   **Architecture:** We employed an Hourglass Diffusion Transformer (HDiT) operating on pixel space.
    *   **Conditioning:** We utilized a pre-trained DINOv2-large model to extract global CLS tokens (1024 dim) and local feature maps ($55 \times 55 \times 1024$).
    *   **Strand Representation:** Individual strands were compressed into a latent code $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{64}$ using a Strand VAE. Strands consisted of 256 points.
    *   **Scalp Texture:** Resolution of $256 \times 256$ pixels.
    *   **Training Strategy:** We used Classifier-Free Guidance with a 10% drop probability to enable both conditional and unconditional generation.
    *   **Loss Weighting:** We implemented a channel-weighting scheme based on perceptual change, with a perturbation strength $\epsilon$ set empirically to 0.8.

## 2. Raw Numeric Data

**Table 1: Quantitative comparison on the Yuksel et al. dataset (Straight and Curly hairstyles)**

| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| NeuralHDHair | 47.91 | 65.07 | 73.76 | 31.59 | 51.10 | 64.63 | 38.00 | 57.12 | 68.73 |
| HairStep | 40.88 | 55.99 | 64.07 | 32.16 | 44.96 | 53.15 | 35.50 | 49.06 | 57.20 |
| Ours | 43.60 | 68.30 | 81.79 | 34.97 | 58.27 | 71.79 | 38.35 | 62.41 | 76.20 |

**Table 2: Quantitative comparison on the DiffLocks evaluation set (10 representative hairstyles)**
| Method | Precision (2mm/20°) | Precision (3mm/30°) | Precision (4mm/40°) | Recall (2mm/20°) | Recall (3mm/30°) | Recall (4mm/40°) | F-score (2mm/20°) | F-score (3mm/30°) | F-score (4mm/40°) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| NeuralHDHair | 18.65 | 36.21 | 49.46 | 19.26 | 37.33 | 51.60 | 18.55 | 35.76 | 49.30 |
| HairStep | 20.22 | 35.54 | 45.73 | 20.80 | 38.53 | 52.82 | 19.42 | 34.38 | 45.48 |
| Ours | 63.06 | 84.16 | 92.78 | 57.91 | 79.71 | 89.81 | 60.13 | 81.68 | 91.17 |

**Table 3: Runtime Performance Comparison (in seconds)**
| Processing Stage | HairStep (s) | NeuralHDHair (s) | Ours (s) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| RGB features | 3.17 | 4.86 | 0.10 |
| Hair model | 0.45 | 4.99 | 1.83 |
| Strand creation | 49.78 | 8.47 | 0.40 |
| **Total Time** | **53.40** | **18.32** | **2.33** |

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Model Performance and Reconstruction Quality**
*   **General Capability:** The diffusion model successfully generated accurate 3D strands from single RGB images. Despite being trained on synthetic data, the method generalized effectively to in-the-wild real images.
*   **Comparison with Baselines:**
    *   *NeuralHDHair and HairStep:* We observed that these methods tended to create hair lacking fine-grained detail. They struggled with curls, often reconstructing strands that ran parallel to each other. They failed to correctly reconstruct balding patterns and afro-like hairstyles.
    *   *HAAR:* While adapted using LLaVA for image-to-text, this method frequently failed to match the specific hairstyle present in the input image.
    *   *Ours:* Our method produced high-quality, realistic hair strands across a wide variety of images, including challenging cases like afro-textures and balding patterns.
*   **Backside Reconstruction:** We observed that our method reconstructed the unseen backside of the hair more faithfully than baselines, attributing this to the strong prior learned from the diverse dataset.

**Ablation Studies and Architecture Analysis**
*   **Scalp Interpolation:** We found that embedding strands onto the scalp texture left gaps. Implementing a push-pull interpolation algorithm successfully created a smooth scalp texture, allowing for valid probabilistic sampling at any density location.
*   **Conditioning Signals:**
    *   *Global-only:* Removing the local feature map and relying solely on the global CLS token caused the generated hair to deviate significantly from the input image.
    *   *Local + Global:* The combination of local feature maps and global tokens captured the most detail.
*   **Generative Model Choice:** Replacing the diffusion model with a VAE (similar to prior work) resulted in reconstructions that were overly smooth and lacked local detail.
*   **Unconditional Generation:** Because we trained with Classifier-Free Guidance, the model successfully generated diverse, high-quality hairstyles without any image input (unconditional mode).

**Data and Rendering**
*   **Dataset Diversity:** The synthetic generation pipeline successfully produced significant variation in length, curliness, and density from a small set of guide strands.
*   **Rendering Integration:** The resulting 3D hair strands were directly compatible with standard engines. We demonstrated real-time rendering in Unreal Engine (running at 60FPS) and offline rendering in Blender, including physics simulations.

[AVAILABLE FIGURES]
### AVAILABLE FIGURES LIST

  - Caption: Figure 1. Given a single RGB image DiffLocks generates accurate 3D strands using a diffusion model. The model is trained on a novel synthetic hair dataset containing RGB images and corresponding 3D strands.

In order to enable probabilistic sampling of strands, we interpolate the sparse strand embeddings to achieve a smooth scalp texture that can be sampled at any position according to the density.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 3:
  - Filename: figure_6.png
  - Caption: Figure 6. Rendering/Simulation. Our generated hair can be directly imported into Blender or Unreal Engine as an Alembic file. In Unreal Engine, the hair can be rendered in real-time with highquality physics simulation (see Supplemental Video).
--------------------------------------------------
Item 4:
  - Filename: figure_7.png
  - Caption: Figure 7. Qualitative comparison. We compare our method with HairStep [55], NeuralHDHair [48] and HAAR [42] on real images. Our method can robustly reconstruct a large variety of hairstyles with significantly more detail than previous approaches. We note that HAAR was designed to reconstruct hair given text captions, so we use LLaVA [19] to obtain text description of hair, followed by applying their text-to-3D method.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 5:
  - Filename: figure_2.png
  - Caption: Figure 2. Method. Given a single RGB image, we use a pretrained DINOv2 model to extract local and global features, which are used to guide a scalp diffusion model. The scalp diffusion model denoises a density map and a scalp texture containing latent codes for strand geometry. Finally, we probabilistically sample texels from the scalp texture and decode the latent code z into strands of 256 points. Decoding in parallel 100K strands yields the final hairstyle.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 6:
  - Filename: figure_8.png
  - Caption: Figure 8. Unconditional generation. We train our diffusion model with Classifier-free Guidance [10] so that the same model can be evaluated both conditionally and unconditionally. Here we show unconditionally generated results where we observe a range of high-quality and diverse hairstyles.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 7:
  - Filename: figure_9.png
  - Caption: Figure 9. Ablation of conditioning signal and model architecture. Removing the local conditioning in the form of feature map Fmap and relying only on the global CLS token severely affects the ability to reconstruct hair. Also generating scalp textures using a VAE yields overly smooth reconstructions. The combination of diffusion and local+global conditioning captures the most detail.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 8:
  - Filename: figure_4.png
  - Caption: Figure 4. Base hairstyles. Starting from a coarse set of guide strands, our Blender pipeline is able to generate a wide variety of hairstyles, covering different lengths, curliness and density patterns. Best viewed zoomed in.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 9:
  - Filename: figure_3.png
  - Caption: Figure 3. Synthetic data. Sample RGB images from our synthetic hair dataset. Each sample from the dataset contains an image at 768× 768 resolution together with the corresponding 3D strand geometry of ≈ 100K strands.
--------------------------------------------------

Figures are located in the figures/ directory and should be referenced appropriately in the paper using standard \includegraphics commands.

prompt.text:
Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

## Example Code for Tables

  \begin{tabular}{@{}lc@{}}

    Method & Frobnability \\
    \midrule
    Theirs & Frumpy \\

  \label{tab:example}
\end{table}
```

   \caption{Example of caption.
   It is set in Roman so that mathematics (always set in Roman: $B \sin A = A \sin B$) may be included without an ugly clash.}
   \label{fig:onecol}
\end{figure}

    \fbox{\rule{0pt}{2in} \rule{.9\linewidth}{0pt}}
    \caption{An example of a subfigure.}
    \label{fig:short-a}
  \end{subfigure}
  \hfill

    \fbox{\rule{0pt}{2in} \rule{.9\linewidth}{0pt}}
    \caption{Another example of a subfigure.}
    \label{fig:short-b}
  \end{subfigure}
  \caption{Example of a short caption, which should be centered.}
  \label{fig:short}
\end{figure*}
```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \centering
\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
   \usepackage{graphicx} ...
   \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]
                   {myfile.pdf}
\end{verbatim}}
```

## Color
If you use color in your plots, please keep in mind that a significant subset of reviewers and readers may have a color vision deficiency; red-green blindness is the most frequent kind.
Hence avoid relying only on color as the discriminative feature in plots (such as red \vs green lines), but add a second discriminative feature to ease disambiguation.


## Important Rules 
* DO NOT change `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleveref}` into `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleverref}`, as there's no `cleverref.sty`.
* Keep the existing packages in the template unchanged.
* For consistent compilation across environments, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command. Failing to include this prefix (e.g., using `figure_1.png` instead of `figures/figure_1.png`) will result in figure loading errors during the build process.
* Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai


Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-11. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 8 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-11.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
The creation of digital humans requires realistic 3D hair geometry. While multi-view capture systems can produce high-fidelity results, they are prohibitively expensive and complex. Consequently, single-view reconstruction—generating 3D hair from a single RGB image—is highly desirable. However, current single-view methods face severe technical limitations.

Existing approaches predominantly rely on low-dimensional intermediate representations, such as guide strands or 2D orientation maps (Gabor filters). These representations compress the geometric complexity of hair, necessitating post-processing steps like upsampling or noise injection to achieve density. This results in two critical failures:
1.  **Loss of Detail:** By modeling only sparse guide strands, these methods fail to capture complex spatial relationships, resulting in over-smoothed, "plate-like" hair clumps rather than individual strands.
2.  **Geometric Limitation:** They fundamentally fail to reconstruct high-frequency geometries, such as tightly curled or afro-like hairstyles, and struggle with diverse density patterns like male pattern baldness.

Furthermore, the field suffers from a data bottleneck. Current datasets lack sufficient scale and diversity in paired RGB-to-3D examples, forcing researchers to rely on restrictive priors.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **DiffLocks**, a generative framework that reconstructs high-fidelity 3D hair strands directly from a single image without guide strands or orientation maps.

Our core hypothesis is that we can treat 3D hair generation as a texture synthesis problem in a canonical UV space. By encoding individual 3D hair strands into a compact latent space and mapping them to a "Scalp Texture," we can train a diffusion model to predict the latent code for *every* hair strand on the head simultaneously.

We hypothesize that:
1.  **Dense Latent Regression:** Directly predicting a dense map of latent codes (where each texel represents a strand) will allow us to model complex, high-frequency curly hairstyles that guide-strand methods cannot represent.
2.  **Semantic Conditioning:** Conditioning the diffusion model on deep semantic features (DINOv2) rather than low-level orientation maps will provide robust guidance for hair growth direction and structure, even under occlusion.
3.  **Synthetic Data Scaling:** By procedurally generating a massive dataset (40K+ hairstyles) with physics-based realism, we can train this model to generalize to in-the-wild real images.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

### 1. Large-Scale Synthetic Data Generation
To address the data scarcity, we will engineer a procedural generation pipeline within Blender.
*   **Scalp Definition:** We will utilize the SMPL-X neutral body model, extracting a scalp mesh of 513 vertices and UV-unwrapping it into a single chart using As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) parametrization.
*   **Procedural Geometry:** We will design a geometry node network that accepts coarse guide strands (approx. 50) and applies operations including interpolation (to 100K strands), clumping, curling, and noise injection.
*   **Physics & Rendering:** We will apply cloth simulation for gravity and wind effects. We will render $768 \times 768$ RGB images using path tracing, randomizing lighting (HDRI), camera parameters, and textures to ensure domain generalization.

### 2. Hairstyle Parameterization

We must compress the high-dimensional 3D hair data into a format suitable for a 2D diffusion model.

#### A. Strand VAE
We formally represent a single hair strand $\mathbf{S}$ as a sequence of $L=256$ 3D points: $\mathbf{S} = \{ \mathbf{p}_1, \mathbf{p}_2, \dots, \mathbf{p}_L \}$.
We will train a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) to compress $\mathbf{S}$ into a latent code $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{64}$.
*   **Encoder $\mathcal{E}$:** A series of 1D convolutions.
*   **Decoder $\mathcal{G}$:** A modulated SIREN (Sinusoidal Representation Network) that maps $\mathbf{z}$ back to $\mathbf{S}$.

**Curvature Loss Formulation:**
Standard position loss is insufficient for curly hair. We will introduce a curvature loss based on the instantaneous change in direction.
We define direction at point $i$ as $\mathbf{d}_i = \mathbf{p}_{i+1} - \mathbf{p}_i$.
We define local curvature as $\boldsymbol{\kappa}_i = \mathbf{d}_{i+1} - \mathbf{d}_i$.
The curvature loss is the L1 distance between the ground truth and predicted curvature:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{cur} = \sum_{i=0}^{L} \lvert \boldsymbol{\kappa}_i - \tilde{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}_i \rvert $$
where $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}_i$ is the curvature of the predicted strand.

The total VAE loss will be:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{VAE} = \sum_{i=0}^{L} \lvert \mathbf{p}_i - \tilde{\mathbf{p}}_i \rvert + \lambda_1 \lvert \mathbf{d}_i - \tilde{\mathbf{d}}_i \rvert + \lambda_2 \lvert \boldsymbol{\kappa}_i - \tilde{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}_i \rvert + \lambda_{KL} \mathcal{L}_{KL} $$

#### B. Neural Scalp Texture
We will parameterize the entire hairstyle as a 2D texture map $\mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 256 \times 64}$.
For each strand in the dataset, we encode it to $\mathbf{z} = \mathcal{E}(\mathbf{S})$ and assign it to the texel corresponding to the strand's root location on the UV-unwrapped scalp.
*   **Density Map:** We also compute a density map $\mathbf{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 256 \times 1}$ with values in $[0, 1]$, representing the probability of hair presence.
*   **Interpolation:** To handle sparse regions (where a texel might not have a strand root), we will apply a push-pull algorithm to interpolate latent codes, ensuring a dense texture $\mathbf{T}$ suitable for convolution.

### 3. Conditional Scalp Diffusion

We will train a conditional diffusion model to generate the scalp texture $\mathbf{T}$ and density map $\mathbf{D}$ given an input image.

#### Architecture
We will utilize an **Hourglass Diffusion Transformer (HDiT)**, optimized for pixel-space diffusion.
*   **Target:** The clean signal is $\mathbf{y} = [\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{D}]$.
*   **Input:** The noised signal is $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y} + \mathbf{n}$, where $\mathbf{n} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 \mathbf{I})$.

We adopt the EDM formulation, parameterizing the denoiser $\mathcal{D}_\theta$ as:
$$ \mathcal{D}_\theta(\mathbf{x}; \sigma) = c_{skip}(\sigma)\mathbf{x} + c_{out}(\sigma)\mathcal{F}_\theta(c_{in}(\sigma)\mathbf{x}; c_{noise}(\sigma)) $$

#### Perceptually-Weighted Loss
Standard MSE on the latent code $\mathbf{z}$ is suboptimal because not all dimensions of $\mathbf{z}$ contribute equally to the strand's shape. We will implement a weighted loss where the weights $\mathbf{w}$ correspond to the perceptual impact of each latent dimension.
We calculate weight $w_i$ by perturbing the $i$-th dimension of a zero-latent $\mathbf{z}_0$ by $\epsilon$ and measuring the geometric distortion in the decoded strand:
$$ w_i = \mathcal{L}_{strand}(\mathbf{S}_0, \mathcal{G}(\mathbf{z}_0 + \epsilon \cdot \mathbf{j}_i)) $$
where $\mathbf{j}_i$ is a one-hot vector. The final loss is:
$$ \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_\theta, u) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{n}, \sigma} \left[ \frac{\mathbf{w}}{e^{u(\sigma)}} \| \mathcal{D}_\theta(\mathbf{y} + \mathbf{n}; \sigma) - \mathbf{y} \|_2^2 + u(\sigma) \right] $$
Here, $u(\sigma)$ represents a learnable log-variance to balance uncertainty across noise levels.

#### Conditioning (DINOv2)
Instead of orientation maps, we will extract robust semantic features using a pretrained **DINOv2-large** model.
*   **Local Features:** $\mathcal{F}_{map} \in \mathbb{R}^{55 \times 55 \times 1024}$. We will inject these via cross-attention layers before each downsampling block in the HDiT, allowing the network to spatially attend to relevant image regions.
*   **Global Features:** The CLS token $\mathcal{F}_{cls} \in \mathbb{R}^{1024}$ will modulate the network globally, similar to the time embedding.
*   **Classifier-Free Guidance:** We will implement random dropout (10%) of the conditioning signal to enable tunable guidance during inference.

### 4. Inference and Reconstruction
During inference, the diffusion model predicts the clean scalp texture $\mathbf{T}$ and density $\mathbf{D}$.
1.  We probabilistically sample texel locations based on the predicted density $\mathbf{D}$.
2.  We extract the latent code $\mathbf{z}$ at each sampled location via bilinear interpolation.
3.  We decode each $\mathbf{z}$ using the Strand VAE decoder $\mathcal{G}$ to obtain the explicit 3D geometry of 100K strands.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **High-Fidelity Curly Hair Reconstruction:** By moving from guide strands to a dense latent texture representation, we expect to be the first single-view method capable of reconstructing high-frequency geometric details like afro hairstyles.
2.  **End-to-End Latent Diffusion:** We provide a framework that bypasses the need for orientation maps and post-processing heuristics (upsampling/densification), offering a direct path from pixels to dense 3D geometry.
3.  **Comprehensive Dataset:** We will release the largest synthetic 3D hair dataset (40K samples) with paired path-traced renderings, addressing the critical data shortage in the field.
4.  **Robust Scalp Representation:** The proposed density map integration allows for the realistic modeling of variable hair distribution, including baldness patterns, which current methods fail to address.

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.

preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
